title: Anointed, Betrayed, Arrested, Condemned, Denied
summary: Two days before Passover the chief priests plot Jesus' death, a woman anoints him at Bethany, and Judas agrees to betray him. Jesus eats the Passover with the Twelve, gives them bread and cup as his body and his blood of the covenant, and predicts their desertion. In Gethsemane he prays in anguish while his disciples sleep, and Judas arrives with an armed crowd. Tried at night before the high priest and council, Jesus declares that he is the Christ and is condemned, while in the courtyard Peter denies him three times.
story:
The whole Gospel has been moving toward this night. Three times Jesus predicted that the Son of Man would be handed over, condemned, and killed (8:31, 9:31, 10:33-34); now it happens step by step, and the verb for handing over, paradidōmi, runs through the chapter from Judas's offer (verse 10) to the arrest (verses 41 to 44). Chapter 13 ended with the command to keep watch, because the master might come in the evening, at midnight, at cockcrow, or in the morning. This chapter moves through exactly those hours: the meal in the evening, Gethsemane in the night, Peter's denial at cockcrow, and, at the start of chapter 15, the handing over to Pilate in the morning.

The chapter also brings the disciples' story to its lowest point. The Twelve were appointed ‘to be with Him’ (3:14); now one betrays him for money, three sleep while he prays, all flee when he is arrested, and their leader swears he does not know him. Against that failure stand two figures. An unnamed woman gives him everything she has, and Jesus himself goes toward the cross with open eyes, arranging the meal, naming the betrayer, praying for the cup to pass and accepting it, and at last breaking his silence to confess before the high priest who he is. Even here he promises restoration: after he is raised he will go ahead of them into Galilee (verse 28), a promise the young man at the tomb repeats in 16:7.
historical:
Passover (Hebrew pesach, Greek pascha) remembered Israel's deliverance from Egypt (Exodus 12). The lambs were slaughtered in the temple on the afternoon of 14 Nisan, in March or April, and eaten that night, which by Jewish reckoning was already 15 Nisan; the seven-day Feast of Unleavened Bread followed (Leviticus 23:5-8), and by the first century the two names were used for the whole festival. Pilgrims crowded into Jerusalem. Josephus reports that at one Passover in the 60s the priests counted 256,500 lambs for the governor Cestius Gallus (Jewish War 6.422-425); the figure is surely inflated, but it shows a city swollen far beyond its normal size. Crowds and a feast of liberation under Roman rule made Passover dangerous. Josephus tells of a riot at Passover under the governor Cumanus, around AD 48 to 52, in which many were crushed to death (Jewish War 2.224-227), which explains the leaders' fear of an uproar (verse 2).

The high priest, whom Mark does not name, was Joseph called Caiaphas, appointed by the prefect Valerius Gratus around AD 18 and removed by the Syrian legate Vitellius around 36 or 37 (Josephus, Antiquities 18.35, 18.95). His long tenure overlapped almost exactly with Pilate's, which implies a working relationship. In 1990 a family tomb in south Jerusalem yielded an ornate ossuary inscribed with the name Joseph son of Caiaphas, which many scholars identify as his. The Sanhedrin was Jerusalem's supreme council, made up of chief priests, elders, and scribes, with the high priest presiding. Under the Roman prefects it handled religious and civil matters, but according to John 18:31 it could not carry out a death sentence on its own authority, which is why the case goes to Pilate at dawn.

Whether the hearing was lawful is an old question. The Mishnah's tractate Sanhedrin, compiled around AD 200, requires capital cases to be tried by day, requires a second day before a guilty verdict, forbids such trials on the eve of a Sabbath or festival (m. Sanhedrin 4:1), voids testimony when witnesses contradict each other (5:2), and defines blasphemy narrowly as pronouncing the divine name (7:5). Measured by those rules, the night hearing of verses 53 to 65 breaks several. Jewish scholars such as Joseph Klausner (Jesus of Nazareth, Hebrew 1922, English 1925), Paul Winter (On the Trial of Jesus, 1961), and Haim Cohn, a justice of Israel's Supreme Court, in The Trial and Death of Jesus, argued in different ways that a Jewish court would not have acted as the Gospels describe, and that responsibility lay mainly with Rome and a few collaborating priests. Herbert Danby (Journal of Theological Studies, 1919) and later Raymond Brown (The Death of the Messiah, 1994) argued that the Mishnah reflects the idealized law of the rabbis after AD 70, not the practice of a Sadducean priestly council in the 30s. Mark himself presents the hearing as a proceeding whose verdict was settled before it began (14:1, 14:55), and he shows that even by the court's own standard the witnesses failed.
cultural:
Guests at a festive meal reclined on couches or cushions, leaning on the left elbow with their feet away from the table, and the Mishnah requires even the poorest Israelite to recline at Passover as a sign of freedom (m. Pesachim 10:1). Anointing a guest's head with perfumed oil was an act of honor (Psalm 23:5), and anointing a head also recalled the anointing of kings (1 Samuel 10:1). Nard came from a plant of the Himalayan region and was imported through India; Pliny the Elder discusses its high price and its adulteration (Natural History 12.42-43). Three hundred denarii was about a year's wages for a day laborer. An alabaster flask had a long neck that could be broken to pour out the whole contents at once. Simon ‘the Leper’ (verse 3) was presumably known by a disease he no longer had, since a man with active tsaraat could not host a dinner.

The Passover meal followed an order that the Mishnah describes in its final form (m. Pesachim 10): blessings over four cups of wine, unleavened bread, bitter herbs, a dish of sauce for dipping, the roasted lamb, a son's questions and the father's retelling of the exodus, and the singing of the Hallel psalms (Psalms 113 to 118), the first part before the meal and the second after it. Rabban Gamaliel is recorded as saying that whoever has not explained three things, the Passover lamb, the unleavened bread, and the bitter herbs, has not fulfilled the duty (m. Pesachim 10:5). How much of this order was fixed in Jesus' day is debated, but the pattern of a host interpreting the food of the meal is exactly what Jesus does with the bread and the cup. The ‘hymn’ of verse 26 was most likely the second half of the Hallel. Carrying water was usually women's work, so a man with a water jar would be easy to spot. Householders in Jerusalem made rooms available to pilgrims, who had to eat the Passover within the city.

Gethsemane means ‘oil press’, and it was an olive grove on the lower slope of the Mount of Olives, across the Kidron valley from the temple. Abba is the Aramaic word for father, used by children and adults alike; its intimacy lies in its use as an address to God, which is rare in surviving Jewish prayer. Disciples greeted their teachers with a kiss, which made Judas's signal both inconspicuous and monstrous. The swords and clubs of the arresting party suggest temple police and servants rather than Roman troops. Tearing one's garments was a sign of grief or horror, and the Mishnah requires judges who hear blasphemy to tear their clothes (m. Sanhedrin 7:5). Galileans spoke Aramaic with a recognizable accent (Matthew 26:73). Finally, the rooster: the Mishnah says chickens were not to be raised in Jerusalem because of purity concerns (m. Bava Kamma 7:7), which has led some to suggest that ‘cockcrow’ was simply the name of the third watch of the night; but the rule may not have been kept, and Mark speaks of a rooster crowing twice.
literary:
Mark frames the chapter with two of his sandwiches, the technique of setting one story inside another so that each interprets the other, which James R. Edwards studied in ‘Markan Sandwiches’ (Novum Testamentum 31, 1989). The first is the priests' plot (verses 1 and 2), the woman's anointing (3 to 9), and Judas's offer (10 and 11): a nameless woman spends a fortune on Jesus while one of the Twelve sells him, and both acts prepare his death. The second is Peter following into the courtyard (54), Jesus on trial inside (55 to 65), and Peter's denials outside (66 to 72). At the very moment Jesus confesses the truth and is mocked with the taunt ‘Prophesy’, his prophecy about Peter is coming true below.

Between the frames the chapter moves by prediction and fulfillment. Jesus predicts that the disciples will find a room (fulfilled in verse 16), that one of them will betray him (fulfilled in 43 to 45), that all will fall away (fulfilled in 50), and that Peter will deny him three times before the rooster crows twice (fulfilled in 66 to 72). Scripture is cited or echoed at each step: Psalm 41:9 at the table, Exodus 24:8 and Isaiah 53:12 in the cup word, Zechariah 13:7 on the road, Psalms 42 and 43 in Gethsemane, and Psalm 110:1 and Daniel 7:13 before the high priest. Jesus says ‘as it is written’ (verse 21) and ‘that the Scriptures would be fulfilled’ (verse 49). The effect is of a man who is not trapped but walking a path he knows.

The Gethsemane scene is built in threes: three disciples taken aside, three prayers, three returns to find them sleeping, which anticipate Peter's three denials. The story of the young man who flees naked (verses 51 and 52) appears only in Mark; its words for ‘young man’ and ‘linen cloth’ return at the burial (15:46) and the tomb (16:5), and readers have proposed that he is the author himself, an echo of Amos 2:16, or a symbol of total desertion. The chapter's two confessions are set against each other. Jesus answers the high priest's question with ‘I am’, and Peter answers a servant girl with ‘I do not know this man’.

doctrines.note: Jesus interprets his death at the table: “This is My blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many” (verse 24). Poured-out blood is the language of sacrifice, and ‘for many’ recalls the servant of Isaiah 53:12 who bore the sin of many. With the ransom saying of 10:45, this is Mark's clearest statement that Jesus' death is given on behalf of others.

The phrase ‘blood of the covenant’ repeats Moses' words at Sinai (Exodus 24:8), with ‘My’ added: the blood that seals this covenant is Jesus' own. Mark does not say ‘new’, but Luke and Paul do (Luke 22:20, 1 Corinthians 11:25), and the cup stands where Sinai and Jeremiah's promise of a new covenant with forgiven sin (Jeremiah 31:31-34) meet.

Here Jesus gives the bread and cup that the church has repeated ever since. Christians agree that he commanded the meal and gives himself in it, but differ on how he is present: Roman Catholic and Orthodox churches confess a change in the elements, Lutherans a real presence in, with, and under them, the Reformed a real spiritual presence received by faith, and many Baptists and others a memorial. These are second-order differences among churches that confess the same Lord.

Gethsemane shows prayer at its most honest: “Abba, Father,” with trust that “all things are possible for You,” with a plain request, “Take this cup from Me,” and with surrender, “Yet not what I will, but what You will” (verse 36). It also shows the disciples' failure to pray and Jesus' warning that a willing spirit is not enough.

Asked whether he is “the Christ, the Son of the Blessed One,” Jesus answers “I am” and adds that they will see the Son of Man at the right hand of Power and coming with the clouds (verses 61 and 62), joining Psalm 110:1 and Daniel 7:13. The secret kept through the Gospel is spoken plainly, and it is the confession for which he is condemned.

words.note: Paradidōmi, to hand over, deliver up, betray. It occurs about 119 times in the New Testament and about twenty times in Mark, seven of them in this chapter. It can describe handing down a tradition, handing someone over to custody, or betrayal. Mark uses it for John's arrest (1:14), in the passion predictions (9:31, 10:33), for Judas (verses 10, 11, 18, 21, 41, 42, 44), and in chapter 15 for the council and Pilate. Paul uses the same verb of God, who ‘delivered Him up for us all’ (Romans 8:32), and of the Son, who gave himself (Galatians 2:20). Behind the human betrayals the reader glimpses a divine giving.

Diathēkē, covenant. It occurs about thirty-three times in the New Testament, seventeen of them in Hebrews, and only here in Mark. In ordinary Greek it could mean a will or testament, but in the Greek Old Testament it translates berit, the binding relationship God established with Noah, Abraham, Israel at Sinai, and David, and the new covenant promised in Jeremiah 31:31. BDAG treats the biblical sense as a declaration of God's will that establishes a relationship. Jesus' ‘blood of the covenant’ places his death where Moses' sacrifice stood at Sinai.

Potērion, cup. It occurs about thirty-one times in the New Testament and six in Mark. At the table Jesus gives the disciples ‘the cup’ of the covenant (verse 23); hours later he asks the Father to ‘take this cup’ from him (verse 36), and he had earlier asked James and John whether they could drink the cup he would drink (10:38). In the prophets the cup is often the cup of God's wrath poured out in judgment (Isaiah 51:17, Jeremiah 25:15). The same word holds together the cup of blessing he gives and the cup of judgment he drinks.

Abba, the Aramaic word for father, kept in Mark's Greek with its translation, ho patēr. It occurs only three times in the New Testament: here on Jesus' lips, and in Romans 8:15 and Galatians 4:6, where Paul says the Spirit enables believers to cry ‘Abba, Father’. Joachim Jeremias argued that such direct address to God was without real parallel in Jewish prayer; James Barr (Journal of Theological Studies, 1988) showed that the word was not simply a toddler's ‘daddy’ but the ordinary word adults also used. Its force lies in the trust with which Jesus uses it at the point of greatest anguish, and in his sharing it with his followers.

Skandalizō, to cause to stumble, to fall away. It occurs about twenty-nine times in the New Testament and eight in Mark. It comes from skandalon, a trap or snare, and in the Gospels it means to be tripped up in faith, to take offense, or to abandon loyalty under pressure. Jesus used it in the parable of the sower for those who fall away ‘when trouble or persecution comes’ (4:17), and in verse 27 he predicts that all the disciples will do exactly that. Peter's protest in verse 29 turns on the same verb.

Aparneomai, to deny, disown. It occurs eleven times in the New Testament, only in the first three Gospels, and four times in Mark: in 8:34, where Jesus calls anyone who would follow him to deny himself, and three times of Peter's denial (verses 30, 31, and 72). The simple verb arneomai is used for the denials themselves (verses 68 and 70). The echo is pointed: Peter, called to deny himself, denies his Lord instead in order to save himself, and the chapter lets the reader feel the cost of both.

Entaphiasmos, preparation for burial. It occurs only twice in the New Testament: here, where Jesus says the woman has anointed his body for burial beforehand (verse 8), and in John 12:7, in John's account of the same event. The related verb describes preparing a body with spices (John 19:40). The perfume itself is muron, costly ointment, used three times in verses 3 to 5. Jesus' interpretation turns an act of honor into the only anointing his body will receive, since the women who come with spices on Sunday find the tomb empty.

christ:
This chapter shows Jesus as the anointed one, the Passover lamb, the covenant sacrifice, the struck shepherd, the obedient Son, and the Son of Man. The title Messiah means anointed one, and the only time Jesus is anointed in Mark is at Bethany, by a woman, for his burial (verse 8). His kingship is marked from the start of the passion as one that goes through death. At the Passover table he speaks of his body and his covenant blood poured out for many, drawing together the lamb of the exodus, the blood of Sinai (Exodus 24:8), and the servant who poured out his life and bore the sin of many (Isaiah 53:12). Paul, writing independently within twenty-five years, calls him ‘our Passover lamb’ (1 Corinthians 5:7). On the road he applies Zechariah 13:7 to himself: God will strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered. Mark's wording, ‘I will strike’, makes God the one who strikes, and Zechariah's next verses promise a refined people who call on God's name, which is why Jesus immediately adds, “But after I have risen, I will go ahead of you into Galilee” (verse 28).

In Gethsemane his full humanity is laid bare. He is ‘deeply troubled and distressed’ and says his soul is sorrowful to the point of death, in words drawn from Psalms 42 and 43. He asks for the cup to pass. Hebrews says that in the days of his flesh he offered prayers with loud cries and tears to the one who could save him from death, and learned obedience through what he suffered (Hebrews 5:7-8). The church drew from this scene its confession that Christ has a true human soul and a true human will, freely surrendered to the Father's will, which the Third Council of Constantinople affirmed in 681. His obedience is not the absence of struggle but its outcome.

In the trial his full identity is declared. Silent before false witnesses, he answers the one question that matters. ‘I am’ is the plainest affirmation of messiahship in Mark, and it may echo the divine self-naming heard when he walked on the sea (6:50). Then he claims the throne beside God of Psalm 110:1 and the everlasting dominion given to the Son of Man in Daniel 7:13, and tells his judges that they will see it. The prisoner will be the judge. And he goes to all of it freely: he arranges the room, names the betrayer, predicts the desertion, rises from prayer to meet the arresting party (‘Rise, let us go’), and refuses to resist. The church has found in this night both the depth of Christ's suffering for sinners and the depth of his faithfulness to the Father.
interpretation:
The words over the bread and cup are the most interpreted lines in this chapter, and their reception begins inside the New Testament. Paul's account in 1 Corinthians 11:23-26, written around AD 54 and handed down, he says, from the Lord, is the earliest written form, and it shares with Luke the command to repeat the act in remembrance. The Didache, a church manual from around AD 100, gives eucharistic prayers of thanksgiving over cup and bread (Didache 9-10), and Justin Martyr, around 155, describes the Sunday Eucharist and says Christians receive the bread and cup not as common food but as the flesh and blood of Jesus (First Apology 66-67). Medieval theology defined the change in the elements as transubstantiation at the Fourth Lateran Council (1215), and the Council of Trent reaffirmed it (Session 13, 1551). The Reformation divided over Mark 14:22 and its parallels. At the Marburg Colloquy of 1529 Luther insisted on the plain ‘is’ and Zwingli read it as ‘signifies’; Calvin (Institutes 4.17) taught a true feeding on Christ by the Spirit through faith. Christians still read these verses differently, and they still receive the meal as Christ's own gift.

Other parts of the chapter shaped doctrine and devotion. The pagan philosopher Celsus mocked Jesus for lamenting and praying to escape death, and Origen answered him (Against Celsus 2.24, around 248) by pointing to the words Celsus left out, ‘not what I will, but what You will’. In the seventh-century controversy over whether Christ had one will or two, Maximus the Confessor made Gethsemane his central text for a true human will surrendered to the divine, and the Third Council of Constantinople (681) adopted that teaching. Oscar Cullmann, in his Ingersoll Lecture of 1955 (published in 1958 as Immortality of the Soul or Resurrection of the Dead?), contrasted Socrates' calm death with Jesus' anguish, arguing that the Bible treats death as an enemy, not a friend. The unnamed woman of Bethany was merged in Western tradition with Mary Magdalene and the sinful woman of Luke 7, a conflation fixed by Pope Gregory the Great's Homily 33 (591) and not adopted by the Eastern churches; Elisabeth Schüssler Fiorenza took the title of her feminist reconstruction of Christian origins, In Memory of Her (1983), from verse 9. Jewish scholars from Joseph Klausner (1922) to Paul Winter (1961) and Haim Cohn studied the trial as a question of Jewish and Roman law, and the Second Vatican Council's declaration Nostra Aetate (1965) stated that what happened in the passion cannot be charged against all Jews then living or against Jews today.

In modern scholarship Joachim Jeremias (The Eucharistic Words of Jesus) argued that the Last Supper was a Passover meal and that its words go back to Jesus; Annie Jaubert (La date de la Cène, 1957) proposed a Tuesday meal on a priestly calendar; Colin Humphreys (The Mystery of the Last Supper, 2011) argued for Wednesday on a reconstructed older calendar; and Raymond Brown's The Death of the Messiah (1994) remains the fullest study of the arrest and trials.

The chapter is at the heart of Holy Week. In the Revised Common Lectionary and the Roman lectionary, Year B, Mark 14:1 to 15:47 is the Passion Gospel for Palm Sunday. Leonardo da Vinci's Last Supper (1495 to 1498), painted on the refectory wall of Santa Maria delle Grazie in Milan, catches the moment when Jesus announces that one of them will betray him (verse 18). Andrea Mantegna and Giovanni Bellini each painted The Agony in the Garden within a few years of each other around 1455 to 1465, and the two panels now hang in the National Gallery, London. Giotto's Kiss of Judas in the Scrovegni Chapel in Padua (about 1305) and Caravaggio's Taking of Christ (1602), recognized in 1990 in a Jesuit house in Dublin and now in the National Gallery of Ireland, show the arrest. Johann Sebastian Bach's St Mark Passion was first performed in Leipzig on Good Friday 1731; its libretto by Picander survives, but the music is lost and has been reconstructed several times.
text:
Several differences among English Bibles in this chapter come from the manuscripts.

In verse 24 some manuscripts, including Codex Alexandrinus and the Byzantine text followed by the King James Version, read ‘my blood of the new covenant’; the earliest witnesses, including Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus, lack ‘new’, which was probably added from Luke 22:20 and 1 Corinthians 11:25. In verse 22 the King James Version adds ‘eat’ after ‘take’, following later manuscripts that assimilated the text to Matthew 26:26. The rooster's two crowings (verses 30, 68, 72) are the most complicated case: some manuscripts, among them Sinaiticus, lack ‘twice’ in verses 30 and 72, and the words ‘and the rooster crowed’ at the end of verse 68 are missing from Sinaiticus and Vaticanus but present in Alexandrinus, Bezae, and many others. Most editors think Mark wrote of two crowings and that scribes brought his text into line with the single crowing of the other Gospels.

In verse 41 Codex Bezae and some other witnesses add ‘the end’ after the obscure word apechei (‘it is enough’), reading ‘the end has come’; most editions keep the shorter text. In verse 62 a small group of manuscripts, including Codex Koridethi (Θ), has Jesus answer ‘You say that I am’, which brings Mark into line with Matthew and Luke; almost all editors accept the plain ‘I am’. In verse 65 the King James Version's ‘did strike him with the palms of their hands’ follows a different verb in later manuscripts from the earlier ‘received Him with slaps’. None of these differences changes the course of the story, but the one in verse 62 affects how directly Jesus answers.

The psalm Jesus echoes in verse 34 is numbered differently in the Greek Old Testament, where Psalms 42 and 43 are counted as 41 and 42, and the psalm behind verse 18 is Psalm 41:9 in English Bibles but 41:10 in the Hebrew, which counts the heading as verse 1.

teach.big: On the night he was handed over, Jesus gave himself freely, interpreting his death as covenant blood poured out for many, embracing the Father's will in anguish, and confessing the truth before his judges, while every human character around him, friend and enemy, failed.

outline.t: Human plotting sets the stage, but the leaders' plan to avoid the feast is overruled: Jesus will die at Passover, on God's timetable, not theirs.
Extravagant love for Jesus is never waste; he receives a woman's gift as preparation for his burial and makes her deed part of the gospel told in all the world.
Betrayal comes from inside the circle, for money, and Mark gives it no excuse, which is why every disciple should ask the question of verse 19.
Jesus is not trapped but in command; the room is ready just as he said, and the Passover he prepares is the setting for his own sacrifice.
The Son of Man goes as it is written, and the betrayer is still responsible: God's purpose and human guilt stand side by side.
At the table Jesus explains his death: his body given, his blood of the covenant poured out for many, and a promise of the kingdom's feast to come.
Jesus knows his friends will fail him, and he promises to go ahead of them before they fail; self-confidence, like Peter's, is no protection.
The Son prays honestly in anguish and yields his will to the Father's, while the disciples sleep; watchfulness requires prayer, because a willing spirit is not enough.
Betrayed with a kiss, Jesus refuses violence and submits so that the Scriptures are fulfilled, and every follower flees, down to the last young man.
Before a court that has already decided, Jesus stays silent against lies and speaks only to confess the truth: he is the Christ, and his judges will see him enthroned.
Peter, who swore he would die with Jesus, disowns him before a servant girl; his tears are where repentance begins, and the risen Lord will name him again (16:7).

teach.pitfalls:
Several misreadings recur. The first uses verse 7, ‘The poor you will always have with you’, to excuse indifference to poverty. Jesus is echoing Deuteronomy 15:11, which in context commands open-handed generosity because the poor will not cease from the land, and he adds that his hearers can help them whenever they want. The second treats the Lord's Supper debates as the chapter's only subject, or presents one tradition's reading of ‘This is My body’ as the plain and only sense. Teachers should state their church's view honestly while acknowledging that faithful Christians read the words differently.

A third error turns Gethsemane into a picture of Jesus' fear of physical pain alone, or, in the opposite direction, into a scene with no real struggle. The text shows real anguish and real submission, and the cup in the prophets is God's judgment, not only suffering. A fourth makes Peter a figure of contempt or a model of mere weakness; Mark tells his failure in full because the church's leader was restored by grace, and every reader stands where Peter stood. A fifth, with a long and shameful history, uses the trial to blame the Jewish people as a whole for Jesus' death. Mark names specific leaders acting from fear and envy, and in the next chapter a Roman governor passes sentence and Roman soldiers carry it out; the church has confessed since the Roman Catechism of 1566 that sinners, including Christians, are the authors of Christ's sufferings. Finally, do not build much on the young man of verses 51 and 52; the text does not say who he was.
teach.pastoral: This chapter presses on people who have been betrayed by someone close, and on people who have betrayed. Judas was one of the Twelve and shared the dish; Peter swore loyalty and broke it within hours. Some in the room will recognize the first experience and need to hear that Jesus knew betrayal from within and did not answer it with violence. Others carry the second and need to hear that Peter's tears were not the end of his story. Gethsemane speaks to anyone facing suffering they did not choose, a diagnosis, a loss, a trial: Jesus' prayer gives permission to ask plainly for the cup to pass and models the surrender that does not pretend. Be gentle with the scrupulous, who may hear ‘Could you not watch one hour?’ as condemnation of every lapse in prayer; Jesus' next words explain the weakness of the flesh with compassion, and he goes to the cross for those who slept. And be careful with the anointing woman: some in the room have been told their devotion is excessive or foolish, and Jesus calls it ‘a beautiful deed’.

hard.q: Was the Last Supper a Passover meal? John seems to place Jesus' death on the day the Passover lambs were killed.
hard.a:
The objection is that the Gospels contradict each other on the date of the crucifixion. Mark, followed by Matthew and Luke, presents the Last Supper as a Passover meal, eaten on the evening after the lambs were sacrificed (verse 12), so that Jesus dies on 15 Nisan, the feast day itself. John says that on the morning of the trial the priests had not yet eaten the Passover (John 18:28) and that Jesus was sentenced on ‘the day of Preparation for the Passover’ (John 19:14), so that he dies on 14 Nisan, as the lambs are slaughtered. The Babylonian Talmud also remembers that Yeshu was executed on the eve of Passover (b. Sanhedrin 43a). Many critical scholars conclude that one account, usually the Synoptic one, has turned a meal held before Passover into a Passover meal, or that John has moved the date to present Jesus as the Passover lamb (compare John 19:36).

Three kinds of answer have been offered. Joachim Jeremias (The Eucharistic Words of Jesus) argued at length that the meal had the marks of a Passover: it was eaten at night, within Jerusalem, reclining, with wine, a dish for dipping, words interpreting the food, and a hymn at the end, and he read John's phrases loosely. Others, including many conservative harmonizers, argue that John's ‘eat the Passover’ in 18:28 refers to the festival's other sacrificial meals during the week and that ‘Preparation of the Passover’ in 19:14 means the Friday of Passover week, so that John and the Synoptics agree. A third group appeals to different calendars: Annie Jaubert (1957) suggested that Jesus followed the priestly solar calendar known from Jubilees and Qumran and ate the meal on Tuesday evening, and Colin Humphreys (2011) proposed a Wednesday meal on an older lunar calendar. Still others, such as Raymond Brown, judge that Jesus held a farewell meal with Passover overtones the evening before the official Passover. No solution commands general agreement. All four Gospels agree that Jesus died at Passover, on a Friday, and that his death was understood in the light of the exodus deliverance.

hard.q: If Jesus was the Son of God, why did he dread death and ask to escape it?
hard.a:
The objection was first put in writing by the pagan philosopher Celsus in the second century, whom Origen quotes: why does he mourn and lament and pray to escape the fear of death, saying, ‘Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me’? A divine being, Celsus implied, would not tremble, and a true philosopher would not either. Socrates, in Plato's Phaedo, drank the hemlock calmly and spoke of death as the soul's release. Later critics have pressed the point in two directions: either Jesus' anguish shows he was an ordinary man who did not expect to rise, or the church's claim that he was God makes the anguish a pretense. Some early Christians shared the embarrassment; Luke 22:43-44, with the angel and the sweat like drops of blood, is missing from several early manuscripts, and some scholars think those verses were either added or removed by scribes troubled by the scene.

Origen answered Celsus (Against Celsus 2.24) by pointing to the words Celsus omitted, ‘not what I will, but what You will’, and by insisting that Jesus' human soul truly felt the sorrow the text describes. The church later made that insistence a matter of confession. Maximus the Confessor, in the seventh century, argued that Gethsemane shows a true human will in Christ, recoiling naturally from death and freely yielding to the divine will, and the Third Council of Constantinople (681) confessed two wills in Christ, the human always submitting to the divine. Oscar Cullmann (Immortality of the Soul or Resurrection of the Dead?, 1958) argued that the contrast with Socrates is exactly the point: the Bible treats death not as a release but as the last enemy, separation from the God of life, so Jesus faced it as the horror it is. Many theologians add that the cup he dreaded was not only death but the judgment the prophets called the cup of God's wrath (Isaiah 51:17), borne for others. Hebrews 5:7-9 says he offered prayers with loud cries and tears and learned obedience through suffering. On this reading Gethsemane shows not the absence of deity but the reality of the incarnation, and the church confesses that the one who prayed there was truly God and truly man.

observe: Mark places the woman's anointing between the priests' plot and Judas's offer (verses 1 to 11). What contrasts do you notice between her and Judas?
List every prediction Jesus makes in this chapter and where each one is fulfilled.
What three things does Jesus say in his prayer in verse 36, and what do the disciples do each time he returns?
interpret: What does Jesus mean by calling the cup ‘My blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many’? How do Exodus 24:8 and Isaiah 53:12 shape the answer?
Why does Jesus stay silent before the false witnesses but answer the high priest's question plainly?
Mark tells Jesus' confession inside the house and Peter's denial outside at the same time. What does the arrangement teach?
apply: The woman was criticized for giving too much. What would it look like for you to give Jesus something others might think excessive?
Jesus prayed, “Yet not what I will, but what You will.” Where are you being asked to pray that prayer now, and what makes it hard?
Peter's failure is told in full, and he is not written off. How does his story shape the way you think about your own failures and the failures of others?
